The campaign succeeded only by foregrounding the 1963 'Dream' King rather than the 1967–68 King who condemned the Vietnam War and called for guaranteed income — the version the Reagan coalition found easiest to quote approvingly. Coretta Scott King noted the irony: the holiday honored the man while the country continued to resist his program.

events.label: The Fall of Saigon
events.description: Saigon fell in April 1975, ending the war that had drained the Great Society, split the movement, and broken Lyndon Johnson. Its end closes the era's long aftermath.

events.label: The 1970 Voting Rights Extension
events.description: Congress renewed and broadened the Voting Rights Act in 1970, and the Supreme Court upheld it, signaling that the era's keystone law would survive the backlash even as busing and affirmative action drew fire.

events.label: The 26th Amendment
events.description: The 1971 amendment lowering the voting age to 18, driven by the argument that those drafted for Vietnam should vote, extended the era's franchise expansion to the young.

events.label: The Orangeburg Massacre
events.description: Police killed three Black students at South Carolina State in February 1968, one of the deadliest and least remembered campus shootings of the era. It prefigured the militarized response to campus protest.

events.label: The Jackson State Killings
events.description: Police killed two students at the historically Black Jackson State College in 1970, days after Kent State, but with a fraction of the national attention. The disparity itself made a point.

events.label: Kent State
events.description: The National Guard's killing of four antiwar students at Kent State in 1970 fused the era's strands of protest, repression, and a war that had consumed the reform agenda.

events.label: Busing Goes National
events.description: By 1972 court-ordered busing to desegregate public schools had become the most divisive racial issue in the country, with Nixon and Wallace running against it and Congress passing non-binding resolutions to limit it. Northern cities that had never had formal legal segregation proved every bit as resistant as the South.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Busing opponents argued that neighborhood schools built communities, while proponents noted that 'neighborhood schools' in practice reflected racially segregated neighborhoods produced by decades of redlining and restrictive covenants. Nixon proposed legislation to freeze court-ordered busing while a constitutional amendment was debated, signaling presidential opposition to his own Justice Department's desegregation enforcement. Polling consistently showed a majority of both Black and white parents preferring neighborhood schools, though for different reasons.

events.label: The Ocean Hill–Brownsville Crisis
events.description: A 1968 fight over community control of schools in a Black Brooklyn district pitted Black parents against a largely Jewish teachers' union, fracturing the Black–liberal alliance in the North.

events.label: An Economic Bill of Rights
events.description: At the heart of the Poor People's Campaign was a demand for an economic bill of rights: a federal guarantee of a job or a living income for every American, large-scale low-income housing, and an end to poverty across race lines. Congress enacted none of it.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The demand for a guaranteed income had been building across the left and some parts of the mainstream since the early 1960s — economist Milton Friedman had proposed a version (a 'negative income tax') from the right, and King's version drew on both that debate and on A. Philip Randolph's 1963 Freedom Budget. The failure in 1968 closed a window; the next serious federal guaranteed-income debate didn't come until the 2020s.

events.label: The Indian Civil Rights Act
events.description: Title II of the 1968 act extended most Bill of Rights protections to Native Americans under tribal government, a reminder that the era's legislation reached beyond the Black–white axis.

events.label: The Chicano and Other Movements
events.description: The Black civil rights movement's tactics, moral vocabulary, and organizing models were picked up across the 1960s and 1970s by the Chicano movement (Mexican-American civil rights and self-determination, from farmworker strikes to student walkouts), and then by Native American, women's, disability, and gay liberation movements. One generation's fight became the grammar for the next.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Chicano Movement explicitly embraced the term 'Chicano' — previously considered a slur — as a mark of pride and collective identity, rejecting assimilation in favor of cultural revitalization. César Chávez's United Farm Workers, one of the movement's anchors, built its power through consumer boycotts (the grape boycott of 1965–1970 drew support from millions of households nationwide) — a direct descendant of the Montgomery Bus Boycott's economic-pressure model.

events.label: The Stonewall Uprising
events.description: The 1969 Stonewall rebellion in New York, often dated to the modern gay-rights movement, drew directly on the civil rights era's model of protest and is part of its long downstream reach.

events.label: The Mule Train
events.description: A wagon train of mule-drawn carts carried poor Southerners to Resurrection City, a deliberate image meant to drag rural Black poverty into the national eye. The era's symbolism was conscious to the end.

events.label: The Look Magazine Confession
events.description: In January 1956, protected by double jeopardy (the rule that you cannot be tried twice for the same crime after an acquittal), Till's killers Roy Bryant and J.W. Milam gave journalist William Bradford Huie a complete, detailed account of exactly how they murdered Emmett Till. Look magazine published it, and the murderers were paid for their story.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Look article, titled 'The Shocking Story of Approved Killing in Mississippi,' ran in the January 24, 1956 issue — less than five months after the acquittal. Bryant and Milam described the entire killing in first-person detail, naming the gin fan they used to weight the body. The confession backfired commercially: both men found themselves shunned even by white Mississippi neighbors and eventually went broke after local businesses refused to deal with them.

events.label: The Prayer Pilgrimage for Freedom
events.description: A 1957 gathering at the Lincoln Memorial, where King gave his 'Give Us the Ballot' speech, rehearsed the March on Washington six years early and put voting at the center of the agenda.

events.label: The Youth Marches for Integrated Schools
events.description: Two large student marches on Washington in 1958–59 for school integration showed young people moving to the front of the movement just before the sit-ins began.

events.label: Black Athletes and the Movement
events.description: From Jackie Robinson to the 1968 Olympic raised-fist protest by Tommie Smith and John Carlos, Black athletes became visible fronts of the struggle, and were punished for it.

events.label: The Deacons for Defense
events.description: The Deacons for Defense and Justice were armed Black men, mostly veterans, who formed in Jonesboro, Louisiana in November 1964 to guard civil rights workers and Black neighborhoods from Klan night-riders. They were the unspoken reason 'nonviolent' campaigns could survive in counties where the Klan operated freely.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Bogalusa, Louisiana chapter was founded on February 21, 1965 — the same day Malcolm X was assassinated — and gained national attention that summer during violent confrontations with the Klan. The Deacons eventually had over 20 chapters across Louisiana, Mississippi, and Alabama. Unlike the NOI's separatism, the Deacons worked alongside CORE and other integrationist groups, embodying the dual-tradition the chapter describes: nonviolent protest on the street, armed protection at the margins.

events.label: Robert F. Williams and 'Negroes With Guns'
events.description: Robert F. Williams was the NAACP branch president in Monroe, North Carolina, and a Marine veteran who armed his chapter with NRA-chartered rifles after courts and police repeatedly failed to protect Black residents from Klan attacks. His 1962 book 'Negroes With Guns,' written in exile, became a direct influence on the Black Panther Party.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Williams's 1957 stand — when his armed members repelled a Klan motorcade attacking a Black doctor's home — was not a spontaneous act of rage; it was organized self-defense by veterans who had trained together. After fleeing the country in 1961, Williams broadcast 'Radio Free Dixie' from Havana and later Beijing, reaching American listeners by shortwave. Fidel Castro personally hosted him in Cuba, and Chinese state media celebrated him as proof that American racial contradictions would eventually destroy the country from within.

events.label: The Federal Mississippi Burning Trial
events.description: In October 1967, a federal jury convicted seven men — including deputy sheriff Cecil Price — of conspiring to deprive the three activists of their civil rights. It was the first time a Mississippi jury had ever convicted white men in a civil rights killing, and the sentences were shockingly light: the maximum given was ten years.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The federal charge was based on an 1870 Reconstruction-era statute because the federal government had no general murder law covering a private killing on state soil; the crime was legally framed as a conspiracy to deprive citizens of constitutional rights, not homicide. Mastermind Edgar Ray Killen, the Klan organizer who planned the murders, escaped conviction in 1967 when one juror refused to convict a preacher — he was finally convicted of manslaughter by a Mississippi state court in 2005, on the 41st anniversary of the murders.

events.label: The Cambridge Movement
events.description: Gloria Richardson led a militant campaign in Cambridge, Maryland that demanded jobs and housing as well as desegregation and refused to disavow self-defense, prefiguring the movement's coming turn.

events.label: The St. Augustine Movement
events.description: Brutal violence against demonstrators in St. Augustine, Florida in mid-1964 helped push the Civil Rights Act over the finish line, a late, less-remembered companion to Birmingham.

events.label: James Bevel and Strategy
events.description: James Bevel was the SCLC's director of direct action and the architect of its three defining campaigns: the 1963 Birmingham Children's Crusade, the 1965 Selma voting-rights movement, and the 1966 Chicago housing marches. He was the movement's most prolific strategic mind, and also one of its least publicly celebrated.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: It was Bevel who proposed the specific idea of a march from Selma to Montgomery after Jimmie Lee Jackson's death — the event that became Bloody Sunday. He had previously conceived the Children's Crusade almost alone, over the skepticism of older SCLC leaders who feared putting children in danger. Bevel also pushed SCLC leadership to call for a March on Washington in 1963, a suggestion that became the march where King delivered 'I Have a Dream.'

events.label: Andrew Young
events.description: Andrew Young was a key SCLC negotiator and strategist who later became a congressman and UN ambassador, embodying the movement's path into electoral and diplomatic power.

events.label: Coretta Scott King
events.description: Coretta Scott King was an activist in her own right who pushed her husband on peace and economic justice and, after his death, fought to keep the radical King from being erased. She built and partly contested his memory.

events.label: Resurrection City Cleared
events.description: After six weeks, police cleared Resurrection City and arrested Abernathy, ending the Poor People's Campaign without the breakthrough King had envisioned. The economic phase of the movement stalled at the start.

events.label: The McCone Commission
events.description: California's official inquiry into Watts blamed rioters and downplayed structural causes, a contrast with the later Kerner Report that showed how contested the meaning of the uprisings was.

events.label: The LDF and the Litigation Front
events.description: The NAACP Legal Defense Fund, the courtroom arm Marshall built, kept winning the cases, from Brown through Green and Swann, that turned street victories into enforceable law. Litigation was a parallel campaign, not a relic.

events.label: Social Science in the Courtroom
events.description: Brown's reliance on psychology and sociology opened a lasting argument over whether courts should decide constitutional questions on social-science evidence, a methodological legacy of the era.

events.label: Measuring the Movement
events.description: Registration statistics, the number of Black elected officials, school-integration percentages, and poverty rates became the era's hard evidence, the data by which its real, partial success can be judged.

events.label: Elijah Muhammad
events.description: Elijah Muhammad ran the Nation of Islam from 1933 until his death in 1975, building it from a small Detroit storefront into a nationwide organization with tens of thousands of members. His theology taught that white people were a race of 'devils' created by an evil scientist — a doctrine that made him a pariah to white America and a magnetic, divisive figure within Black America.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Elijah Muhammad was born Elijah Poole in Georgia and moved north during the Great Migration. He was convicted of draft evasion during World War II and imprisoned from 1942 to 1946 — a period that, paradoxically, boosted the NOI's membership as he preached from behind bars. His personal life became a central reason Malcolm X broke with him: Malcolm discovered Elijah had fathered children with several young secretaries, violating the strict moral code the organization publicly demanded of its members.

events.label: White Clergy and the Movement
events.description: White priests, rabbis, nuns, and ministers, like Abraham Joshua Heschel marching at Selma, joined at real cost, while King's 'Letter' had been addressed to white clergy who urged patience. Religion sat on both sides of the line.

events.label: The Postwar NAACP Surge
events.description: NAACP membership grew roughly tenfold during World War II, building the dues-paying mass base and local chapter network that the postwar campaigns would mobilize.

events.label: The Blinding of Isaac Woodard
events.description: On February 12, 1946, hours after receiving an honorable discharge, Black Army veteran Isaac Woodard was pulled off a bus in South Carolina, beaten by police, and permanently blinded — still in uniform. His case became a national symbol of what Black servicemen faced returning from a war against fascism.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Woodard's assault became public partly through Orson Welles, who read the story over ABC Radio for weeks and named the police chief responsible. The officer was tried in federal court and acquitted in 15 minutes by an all-white jury while the courtroom laughed. President Truman was shown photographs of Woodard's injuries and reportedly told an aide, "My God, I had no idea it was as terrible as that" — a moment historians credit as personally pivotal in Truman's turn toward civil rights.

events.label: The Cicero Race Riot
events.description: A white mob in Cicero, Illinois drove out a Black family in 1951, a Northern reminder that segregation by violence was not a Southern monopoly years before the movement turned north.

events.label: The Black Vote and the 1960 Election
events.description: Kennedy's call to Coretta Scott King while King was jailed helped swing Black votes in a razor-thin election, demonstrating that the re-enfranchising Black electorate could now decide presidencies.

events.label: The Mississippi Freedom Vote
events.description: A 1963 mock election in Mississippi drew some 80,000 disfranchised Black votes, proving the desire to vote was overwhelming and laying the groundwork for Freedom Summer and the MFDP.

events.label: The Big Six
events.description: The March on Washington was run by the 'Big Six' leaders representing the movement's full political range, from the NAACP's legal strategy to SNCC's radicalism — and the strain showed: SNCC's John Lewis was pressured to soften his speech minutes before he spoke.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Lewis's original draft called the Kennedy administration's civil rights bill "too little, too late" and asked "which side is the federal government on?" The Catholic Archbishop of Washington threatened to withdraw from the event unless the language was changed. Lewis agreed to revise — but the original draft leaked, and it was blunter than almost anything else spoken that day.

events.label: Prathia Hall and the Unsung
events.description: SNCC field secretary Prathia Hall, whose 'I have a dream' prayer King reportedly heard before his own speech, stands for the hundreds of local organizers history nearly lost. The movement was made of them.

events.label: Contested Memory and the Record
events.description: From the documentary 'Eyes on the Prize' to a vast archive of oral histories, FBI files, and SNCC papers, the era is one of the best-documented in American history, which is exactly why its sanitized memory is contested.

events.label: Richard Russell and the Filibuster Bloc
events.description: Richard Russell of Georgia was the Senate's most respected parliamentarian and the longtime mentor who had taught Johnson how the chamber worked — and he led the Southern Democratic bloc's disciplined, rotating filibuster against the 1964 act.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Russell had served in the Senate for nearly 40 years and was Governor of Georgia before that, making him one of the most powerful figures in Washington. His strategy against the 1964 bill was not improvisation: he ran it as a precision operation, rotating his senators in platoons so no one would tire while forcing the bill's supporters to remain on call around the clock. He died in 1971 still the most senior member of the Senate.

events.label: The 1964 Cloture Vote
events.description: On June 10, 1964, the Senate voted 71 to 29 to invoke cloture — ending debate and forcing the bill to a vote — for the first time in history on a civil rights measure. Nine days later, the Civil Rights Act passed.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The galleries were packed for the vote. Senator Clair Engle of California, dying of a brain tumor and no longer able to speak, was wheeled onto the floor and cast his 'aye' by pointing to his own eye. Cloture required 67 votes (two-thirds of the Senate at the time), and the motion got 71 — four votes to spare — only because the coalition included both non-Southern Democrats and most Senate Republicans voting together against the Southern bloc.

events.label: The Commerce Clause Hook
events.description: The 1883 Civil Rights Cases had ruled that the Fourteenth Amendment only restrained governments, not private businesses — a loophole that let segregated hotels and lunch counters claim the Constitution didn't reach them. Congress deliberately grounded the 1964 act in the Commerce Clause instead, and the Supreme Court agreed unanimously in Heart of Atlanta Motel, finally closing that loophole.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The 1883 cases struck down the Civil Rights Act of 1875, which had tried to ban discrimination in public accommodations after Reconstruction. The Court's ruling that the Fourteenth Amendment couldn't touch private conduct (as distinct from government action) remained valid precedent and was never overturned — Congress simply went around it by using a different constitutional hook. The Thirteenth Amendment piece of the 1883 ruling was separately overturned in 1968, but the private-action limit on the Fourteenth Amendment still stands today.

events.label: The 'Sex' Amendment
events.description: Virginia Representative Howard Smith, a leader of the Southern conservative bloc and an opponent of the whole civil rights bill, added the word 'sex' to the employment discrimination title on the House floor — an amendment widely read as a sabotage attempt meant to make the bill look absurd and sink it. The bill survived anyway, and the amendment accidentally became the foundation of American sex-discrimination law.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Smith's actual motive is genuinely disputed among historians: he had real ties to the women's rights lobby and had previously introduced equal-pay legislation, so the 'sabotage' reading isn't the only one on offer. Whatever he intended, the amendment passed with support from both conservatives and liberal women's-rights supporters. The result is that Title VII of the 1964 act — the employment discrimination ban — has been the primary legal tool for sex-discrimination cases in the United States ever since.

events.label: The Monroe Stand and Williams's Exile
events.description: In 1961, Robert F. Williams was charged with kidnapping after sheltering a white couple from an angry crowd in Monroe — a charge he said was fabricated. He fled to Cuba, then China, broadcasting 'Radio Free Dixie' for eight years until the charges were dropped and he came home in 1969.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Williams was placed on the FBI's Ten Most Wanted list — an extraordinary status for a civil rights organizer rather than a violent criminal. The kidnapping charge stemmed from a chaotic night of Klan and anti-Klan violence in Monroe; witnesses on all sides gave conflicting accounts and the case was never tried. His years in China overlapped with the Cultural Revolution, during which he met Mao Zedong; he later expressed discomfort with what he witnessed of Maoist politics.

events.label: The Bandung Conference
events.description: In April 1955, twenty-nine newly independent or soon-to-be-independent nations from Asia and Africa — representing 1.5 billion people — gathered in Bandung, Indonesia, to chart a third path between the American and Soviet blocs. The conference crystallized a non-aligned world whose leaders were watching American segregation with disgust.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The twenty-nine governments at Bandung collectively represented 54% of the world's population at the time. Indonesia's President Sukarno opened the conference by explicitly invoking the American civil rights struggle, calling racial discrimination "one of the greatest obstacles to peace." The conference gave rise to the Non-Aligned Movement, which eventually grew to include more than 100 countries.

events.label: The Church Committee Exposes COINTELPRO
events.description: The Senate Select Committee on Intelligence — the Church Committee — investigated U.S. intelligence agency abuses in 1975–76 and published the documented record of COINTELPRO, converting decade-old suspicions into official, sourced fact.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Chaired by Idaho senator Frank Church, the committee's published reports ran to thousands of pages and covered CIA assassination plots, NSA mass surveillance, IRS targeting of political enemies, and FBI domestic disruption. It directly led to the creation of the permanent Senate Intelligence Committee to provide ongoing oversight. The Church Committee's work is why we know as much as we do about what was done to the civil rights movement — before its reports, most of the COINTELPRO operations were still officially denied.

events.label: The First Black Mayors of Major Cities
events.description: In 1973, Maynard Jackson was elected the first Black mayor of Atlanta and Coleman Young the first Black mayor of Detroit, both cities that had experienced devastating race riots in the 1960s. Their elections demonstrated that the Voting Rights Act had converted Black enfranchisement into actual governing power.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Jackson won 59 percent of the vote in Atlanta, a city with a Black majority population by then, and immediately pushed to increase minority contracting on the massive new Hartsfield Airport project, using the city's procurement power as a direct economic-integration tool. Coleman Young, a former labor organizer and target of McCarthy-era investigations, served as Detroit's mayor for an unprecedented twenty years. Their elections in the same year as the Milliken ruling illustrated the chapter's central paradox: desegregation law was being capped just as Black electoral power was becoming durable.

events.label: Mahalia Jackson at the March
events.description: Mahalia Jackson, the most celebrated gospel voice in America, sang at the March on Washington and, by widely reported accounts, called out to King as he neared the end of his prepared remarks — prompting the improvised passage that became the speech's immortal passage.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Jackson had been friends with King for years and performed at many movement events; she was not a bystander but a regular presence in his circle. She sold an estimated 22 million records and had crossed into mainstream commercial success at a time when Black gospel artists rarely did, giving her a platform that made her endorsement of the movement visible to white audiences. Her 1947 recording of "Move On Up a Little Higher" sold over 8 million copies, a gospel industry record at the time.

events.label: The Movement as Global Template
events.description: The Northern Ireland Civil Rights Association, founded in Belfast in April 1967, modeled its marches and tactics directly on the American movement and sang 'We Shall Overcome' at its demonstrations. The global reach of the movement was not metaphorical: activists in Belfast, Johannesburg, and elsewhere studied Selma as a how-to manual.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: NICRA's demands mapped almost exactly onto American civil rights demands: one person, one vote (Northern Ireland had property-based voting that disproportionately excluded Catholics); an end to housing discrimination; abolition of the Special Powers Act (which allowed detention without trial). The contrast with South Africa was instructive: where American civil rights leaders could embarrass the federal government on national television, the ANC faced a white-minority state with no comparable domestic audience to shame, which is part of why nonviolence was abandoned there after the 1960 Sharpeville massacre.
